gaps.sentence: How ___ you speak to me like that!
gaps.hint: outrage with the phrase how dare
gaps.explanation: 'How dare you' expresses outrage at someone's behavior: dare.

gaps.sentence: It is Saturday tomorrow, so I ___ get up early.
gaps.hint: an absence of obligation at weekends
gaps.explanation: 'Don't have to' shows there is no obligation: don't have to get up.

gaps.sentence: He ___ be at work — I've just seen him at the beach.
gaps.explanation: 'Can't' expresses something the evidence rules out.

gaps.sentence: Sorry I am late — I ___ to take my car to the garage this morning.
gaps.explanation: Past obligation uses 'had to', since 'must' has no past form: had to.

gaps.sentence: You ___ pay for children under six — entry is free for them.
gaps.explanation: 'Needn't' expresses absence of necessity: needn't pay.

gaps.sentence: You ___ to see that exhibition before it closes — it is outstanding.
gaps.hint: a strong recommendation with ought to
gaps.explanation: 'Ought to' recommends something strongly: ought to see.

gaps.sentence: You ___ better book now — the prices rise every week.
gaps.explanation: 'Had better' gives strong advice, often with urgency: had better book.

gaps.sentence: They ___ have checked the dates before booking — now they have lost the money.
gaps.explanation: 'Should have' expresses criticism of something not done: should have.
